extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, researchers, and activists in communication studies, political economy, environmental justice, and media/policy advocacy
extracted.subtask_short: framing for social movements and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflection on how to frame problems, use statistical evidence, and deploy information subsidies to influence public opinion and policy—with attention to ethics, methodology, and effects on marginalized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing (problem definition & responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: How you make sense is to say who, what’s the nature of the problem? Who’s responsible for the problem—that is, who caused the problem, but also who is responsible for changing the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames capture attention and move people through a story; effective framing defines the problem clearly and identifies actors responsible for causing and remedying it. Use framing to guide citizen and policy-maker behavior. Anti-pattern: letting stories slip back into dominant cultural assumptions that blunt mobilizing potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of information subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution and shaping of information by powerful actors (information subsidies) affects what stories and frames dominate media and policy discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that corporations and well-resourced actors supply information subsidies that shape policy conversations; activists should design counter-subsidies (framed messages and material for press) to contest dominant narratives. Example: moving from criticizing information subsidies toward deploying them on behalf of under-resourced groups. Anti-pattern: assuming media will pick up a frame without providing tailored information subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical authority in policymaking and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers have a particular purchase and expert authority in policymaking and media representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics confer legitimacy but can mislead if the limits of methods are ignored. Be explicit about what statistics show and do not show; anticipate that journalists and policy actors will treat numbers as authoritative. Scoring note: stronger arguments show how statistics connect to lived harms and distributional effects, not just aggregate trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational discrimination is an economic notion that actors make choices based upon consequences that flow from past data or cues, often without sensitivity to how those choices reproduce past constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purportedly 'rational' data‑based decisions with skepticism when they rely on historic patterns that perpetuate inequality. Explain how seemingly rational choices (e.g., hiring or lending based on averages) can have discriminatory, cumulative effects. Anti-pattern: accepting past-based predictive choices as neutral or objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions perceived as rational can add 'another block' to constraints on development for marginalized groups—harm accumulates rather than being randomly distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using data and prediction, assess impacts on distribution tails and how repeated 'rational' choices compound disadvantage. Policy framing should foreground accumulation of harms and the ways decisions reproduce constraints (education, neighborhood, employment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk framing and insurance logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance and risk discourse specify what policymakers and institutions pay attention to—primarily negative risk (things to avoid) rather than potential benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that an insurance/risk frame privileges avoidance of cost and can narrow policy focus to exclusionary prevention. To broaden discourse, explicitly reframe to include benefits and distributive considerations. Anti-pattern: letting insurance-derived risk logics define social policy choices without equity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic framing for social movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing can be used proactively as a counter-response to dominant information subsidies to mobilize public support and influence policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design frames that resonate with target publics and policymakers; test and iterate frames using evidence-based methods. Work with communication experts (e.g., FrameWorks) to discover what 'works' and to avoid frames that trigger counterproductive assumptions. Measure effectiveness by uptake, resonance, and policy movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of investigative journalism framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism can sometimes undermine efforts to invoke policy responses because journalists select and shape material and may use frames of risk/statistics that diffuse responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When engaging journalists, provide contextualized statistics and clear responsibility attribution; anticipate selective reporting and craft messages that retain the core causal/responsibility frame even if reduced. Anti-pattern: assuming exposure alone yields policy action without attention to framing and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based framing methods (FrameWorks approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: FrameWorks Institute studies framing through surveys, interviews, and experiments to inform progressive organizations about how they ought to frame issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirically tested frames rather than intuition; employ surveys, interviews, and experimental approaches to validate which frames increase understanding and support for policy. Guidance includes learning both what works and what doesn’t, and being ready to adapt language to avoid triggering dominant counterframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neuromarketing inference limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Neuromarketing attempts to understand feelings without depending on self-report, but often relies on too-small samples and costly methods that risk overgeneralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat neuromarketing findings as suggestive, not definitive; scrutinize sample sizes, generalizability, and inferential leaps. Avoid using single or small neural studies to claim population-level effects. Anti-pattern: presenting neural measures as displacing the need for broader, representative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of nudging versus education
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral economics and nudging can be used to manipulate behavior; there is tension between manipulation and educating citizens so they would make choices if fully informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interventions that educate and empower where possible; if using nudges, be explicit about intent and ethical trade-offs. Acknowledge that framing/education efforts themselves can be manipulative and reflect on responsibilities and consent. Scoring note: higher ethical standing when interventions increase autonomy and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid averaging that ignores distribution tails
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and predictions often talk about means (centers of distribution) and thus fail to account for people at both ends of distributions who may be constrained by decisions based on averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting statistics, highlight variance and the existence of outliers; assess impacts on individuals at tails and avoid policies that exclude potential high performers purely due to mean-based cutoffs. Anti-pattern: selection or exclusion decisions based solely on mean predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include race and ethics explicitly in framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert ethics and race (e.g., environmental justice) into discourse so community harm and standing are recognized as racial acts rather than neutral outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft frames that make racial and ethical dimensions visible (e.g., show how pollution decisions were made on a racial basis). Use social identity and institutional rationality analyses to establish standing and culpability. Example: framing community pollution as a racialized decision to support environmental justice claims.
